source_text: EGEON. A heavier task could not have been imposed on me than to speak my unspeakable griefs. Still, so the world may witness that my end was caused by fate, not by any vile crime, I'll tell what my sorrow allows me to say. I was born in Syracuse, and married to a woman who would have been happy — except for me, and through no fault but our bad luck. I lived with her in joy. Our wealth grew through the successful voyages I often made to Epidamnum, until my agent there died and the great burden of unmanaged goods drew me away from my wife's embrace. I had not been gone six months before she — almost ready to faint under the pleasant burden women bear — made arrangements to follow me, and soon arrived safely where I was. She had not been there long before she became the joyful mother of two fine sons, and — strangely — one looked so like the other that they could be told apart only by their names. In that very same hour, and at the same inn, a poor woman gave birth to a similar pair, male twins, also identical. Because their parents were extremely poor, I bought them and raised them to wait on my sons. My wife, not a little proud of two such boys, asked daily that we go home. Reluctantly, I agreed; alas, too soon. We had sailed only a league from Epidamnum before the always-obedient sea gave any tragic sign of our coming disaster. But we soon lost much hope, for what little light the heavens granted only brought to our terrified minds a near-certain warning of immediate death — which I myself would gladly have embraced, but the constant weeping of my wife, weeping in anticipation of what she saw coming, and the pitiful crying of the pretty babies, who cried because that's what they saw us doing without knowing what to fear, forced me to find delays for them and for myself. And it came to this — for there was no other option. The sailors took the lifeboat to save themselves, leaving us the ship, which was on the verge of sinking. My wife, more concerned for the younger-born, had tied him to a small spare mast, the kind sailors keep on board for storms. One of the other twins was bound to him, while I had done the same with the other pair. With the children thus secured, my wife and I, keeping our eyes fixed on the children we cared for, tied ourselves to either end of the mast, and floating along, carried by the current, were swept towards Corinth, as we thought. At last the sun, gazing on the earth, dispersed those threatening clouds, and by the help of its welcome light the seas grew calm. We spotted two ships in the distance, racing toward us — one from Corinth, the other from Epidaurus. But before they reached us — oh, let me say no more! Guess the rest from what came before.
modern_text: EGEON. A heavier task could not have been impos’d Than I to speak my griefs unspeakable; Yet, that the world may witness that my end Was wrought by nature, not by vile offence, I’ll utter what my sorrow gives me leave. In Syracusa was I born, and wed Unto a woman happy but for me, And by me, had not our hap been bad. With her I liv’d in joy; our wealth increas’d By prosperous voyages I often made To Epidamnum, till my factor’s death, And the great care of goods at random left, Drew me from kind embracements of my spouse; From whom my absence was not six months old Before herself (almost at fainting under The pleasing punishment that women bear) Had made provision for her following me, And soon and safe arrived where I was. There had she not been long but she became A joyful mother of two goodly sons, And, which was strange, the one so like the other As could not be distinguish’d but by names. That very hour, and in the self-same inn, A mean woman was delivered Of such a burden, male twins, both alike. Those, for their parents were exceeding poor, I bought, and brought up to attend my sons. My wife, not meanly proud of two such boys, Made daily motions for our home return. Unwilling I agreed; alas, too soon We came aboard. A league from Epidamnum had we sail’d Before the always-wind-obeying deep Gave any tragic instance of our harm; But longer did we not retain much hope; For what obscured light the heavens did grant Did but convey unto our fearful minds A doubtful warrant of immediate death, Which though myself would gladly have embrac’d, Yet the incessant weepings of my wife, Weeping before for what she saw must come, And piteous plainings of the pretty babes, That mourn’d for fashion, ignorant what to fear, Forc’d me to seek delays for them and me. And this it was (for other means was none). The sailors sought for safety by our boat, And left the ship, then sinking-ripe, to us. My wife, more careful for the latter-born, Had fast’ned him unto a small spare mast, Such as sea-faring men provide for storms. To him one of the other twins was bound, Whilst I had been like heedful of the other. The children thus dispos’d, my wife and I, Fixing our eyes on whom our care was fix’d, Fast’ned ourselves at either end the mast, And, floating straight, obedient to the stream, Was carried towards Corinth, as we thought. At length the sun, gazing upon the earth, Dispers’d those vapours that offended us, And by the benefit of his wished light The seas wax’d calm, and we discovered Two ships from far, making amain to us, Of Corinth that, of Epidaurus this. But ere they came—O, let me say no more! Gather the sequel by that went before.

source_text: ADRIANA. Only the unfeeling can shrug off wrongs like these. I know his eye is paying respects elsewhere — what else could be keeping him away from here? Sister, you know he promised me a chain. I'd give up that gift, even a portion of his love, if only he'd keep faith with our bed. I see that even the most beautifully enamelled jewel loses its beauty in time; yet the gold underneath endures even what others touch — though frequent touching will wear gold thin. And no man with a good name shames it through dishonesty and corruption — and yet so it goes. Since my beauty can't please his eye, I'll weep what's left of it away, and weeping, die.
modern_text: ADRIANA. Unfeeling fools can with such wrongs dispense. I know his eye doth homage otherwhere, Or else what lets it but he would be here? Sister, you know he promis’d me a chain; Would that alone, a love he would detain, So he would keep fair quarter with his bed. I see the jewel best enamelled Will lose his beauty; yet the gold bides still That others touch, yet often touching will Wear gold; and no man that hath a name By falsehood and corruption doth it shame. Since that my beauty cannot please his eye, I’ll weep what’s left away, and weeping die.

source_text: DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. O, sir, I did not look so low. To conclude: this drudge or diviner laid claim to me, called me Dromio, swore I was assured to her, told me what privy marks I had about me, as the mark of my shoulder, the mole in my neck, the great wart on my left arm, that I, amazed, ran from her as a witch. And, I think, if my breast had not been made of faith, and my heart of steel, she had transformed me to a curtal dog, and made me turn i’ the wheel.
modern_text: DROMIO OF SYRACUSE. Oh, sir, I didn't look that low. To wrap up: this drudge or diviner laid claim to me, called me Dromio, swore I was promised to her, told me what private marks I had about me — the mark on my shoulder, the mole on my neck, the great wart on my left arm — that I, amazed, ran from her like she was a witch. And I think, if my chest hadn't been made of faith and my heart of steel, she would have transformed me into a stub-tailed dog and made me run in the kitchen wheel.
